row: | | Askell et al., *A General Language Assistant as a Laboratory for Alignment* (2021 ⚑): a 14-conversation HHH prompt lowers HumanEval/QuixBugs scores for small code models but makes the 13B and 52B models noticeably better (Lambada: a small, size-independent tax); ranked preference modelling beats imitation learning and scales better, with little difference on binary tasks; preference-model pretraining on 5.8M StackExchange, 1.1M Reddit and 1.4M Wikipedia-edit pairs improves fine-tuning sample efficiency for models above ~1B, most at 500 pairs; masking imitation-learning loss to the response "improved performance significantly", scored by pairwise comparison, not generation | [2112.00861](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.00861) | ✓ [askell-2021-general-language-assistant-as-laboratory.pdf](sources/askell-2021-general-language-assistant-as-laboratory.pdf) | [RL 02](../05-RL/notes/02-rlhf-pipeline.md#sft-in-practice), [RL 02](../05-RL/notes/02-rlhf-pipeline.md#stage-2--reward-model-training), [RL 02](../05-RL/notes/02-rlhf-pipeline.md#alignment-tax) |

edits.old: prompt cost small models accuracy, but gave a small gain at 13B and 52B
edits.new: prompt cost small models accuracy on the HumanEval and QuixBugs coding evals, but made the 13B and 52B models noticeably better
edits.why: §2.2.4 / Fig. 10: the size-dependent tax-vs-bonus was measured on code-finetuned models on HumanEval and QuixBugs, and the paper calls the large-model effect 'noticeably better', not a small gain; on Lambada (Fig. 7) the prompt imposes a small tax with no significant size dependence. The note gave no setup.

doubts: Three citing passages in one note; I linked the same note three times with different anchors. Other two passages (loss masking §3.1 p.15; PMP sizes App. C.1, 500-pair result §4.2 Fig. 16; ranked vs binary Fig. 1/§3.2) verified as written.

row: | | Shuster et al., *BlenderBot 3* (2022 ⚑): a 175B OPT-based chatbot trained to run search, memory and reply modules via control codes; in public deployment users liked 4.0% of BB3-175B messages, and crowdworkers judged 31% of users' utterances bad, 42% of those rude or inappropriate; on the SAFETY MIX troll benchmark, user-level trust filtering (Per-User+Example Removal) cut post-training error from 31% to 12%; in crowdworker FITS experiments (mostly 3B models), module-level feedback such as a better search query improved models more than feedback on the final reply | [2208.03188](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.03188) | ✓ [shuster-2022-blenderbot-3.pdf](sources/shuster-2022-blenderbot-3.pdf) | [agentic 04](../07-agentic-applications/notes/04-application-patterns.md#interactive-chatbot) |

edits.old: a 175B OPT model whose search decision, query writing, memory and reply are separate prompted modules
edits.new: a 175B model fine-tuned from OPT that runs search decision, query writing, memory and reply as separate modules, each selected by a control code
edits.why: §3.1: 'the modules are not independent components – this is achieved by training a single transformer model to execute the modules, with special control codes in the input context'. They are fine-tuned, not prompted.

doubts: The 31%/42% human-utterance figures come from the BB3-3B deployment sample (Table 9), and the module-feedback finding from the crowdworker FITS study (Table 3, §5.1), not the public 175B deployment; the note blends them under one deployment. Left as is (minor); could add 'in a crowdworker study' after 'Feedback tied to a specific module'.
